chapter: Playing fast, best gigs and the future
title: Jimmy Lovelace and playing really fast tempos
summary: Drummer Jimmy Lovelace showed him you need only be in the vicinity of the changes at very fast tempos.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: It’s really good, because fast tempos, man, it’s all about being in sync. Like I know we talked about “Countdown” before, but let’s just say you want to learn how to play it fast. I used to play with a great drummer, Jimmy Loveless. You know he’s a New York guy, he played with Wes Montgomery and was on some of his records. But he was a real New York cat. And he used to play really fast. And I realized with him that you didn’t have to play every change. You just had to be in the vicinity of that sound. Every once in a while it was so fast [scats] and you didn’t have to play every chord change. You just had to be in the vicinity of it. You had to play your ideas and they had to be crisp and they had to be clear, but they didn’t have to be, you didn’t have to play every bar. You just had to be there. You know, okay there’s the bridge, now play the bridge. You know and then play something. That’s what he found. He didn’t play every chord change. He just marked them. But I’m talking really fast now. I’m not talking like uptempo. I’m talking like [inaudible] on the Sonny Rollins record. That kind of stuff. And sometimes it’s another way to practice. Because you can’t really practice that on a trumpet, it’s hard, to do that at home by yourself. So I used to just put on a record with a fast tempo and then get it really, get it all formed in my brain, you know, understand the form and everything, and then just sit there and think about it.
